# The Productivity Illusion: When Busyness Masks Divergence

A workshop can look productive because everybody is busy. Saws whir, hammers strike, hands move constantly. From the doorway, activity looks like progress. But the appearance of work is not the same thing as work aimed at a shared goal. The people inside may be solving entirely different problems, and no amount of individual effort will reconcile them if their efforts point in different directions. This is one of the most persistent illusions in collaborative settings, whether that setting is a carpentry shop, a research laboratory, a software team, or a hospital ward. The scene hums with energy, yet the energy may be wasted.

Consider a concrete example. Imagine a furniture workshop where a client has commissioned a custom dining table. The master carpenter has interpreted the design as a trestle table with a thick oak top. Two apprentices, working from a brief conversation rather than written specifications, believe they are building a farmhouse-style table with breadboard ends. For several hours, everyone is busy.
